walkthrough:
Start With The Fuel - Reduced Carriers**
Think of reduced NAD and reduced FAD as delivery trucks. They were loaded with hydrogen during glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle. In oxidative phosphorylation they unload - the hydrogen splits into protons ($H^+$) and electrons ($e^-$). The electrons are the useful energy source for what follows.

Electrons Flow And Release Energy**
The site is the inner mitochondrial membrane, folded into cristae to give a large surface area. Embedded there is a chain of electron carriers - the electron transport chain. Electrons hop from one carrier to the next, falling to lower energy levels, so energy is released at each step. A common slip is to say energy is made - it is released from the electrons and then used to do work.

Pump Protons To Build A Gradient**
That released energy is used to pump protons from the mitochondrial matrix across the inner membrane into the intermembrane space. So protons build up to a high concentration there and a low concentration in the matrix. This difference in concentration and charge is the proton gradient, sometimes called the electrochemical gradient.

Chemiosmosis Makes ATP**
The inner membrane is impermeable to protons except through ATP synthase. Protons diffuse down their gradient through ATP synthase - this is chemiosmosis. The flow turns the enzyme and provides energy to phosphorylate $ADP + Pi$ to $ATP$. That is the oxidative part linked to phosphorylation.

Oxygen Keeps The Chain Moving**
At the end of the chain electrons would pile up and block everything. Oxygen acts as the final electron acceptor, picking up electrons plus protons to form water ($2H^+ + 2e^- + 1/2O_2 \rightarrow H_2O$). That is why oxygen is needed for continued aerobic ATP production.

Final answer: Reduced NAD / reduced FAD release hydrogen, which splits into protons and electrons. On the inner mitochondrial membrane / cristae, electrons pass along the electron transport chain, releasing energy. This energy pumps protons into the intermembrane space, establishing a proton gradient. Protons diffuse back through ATP synthase by chemiosmosis, joining ADP + Pi to form ATP. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, forming water.

walkthrough:
Describe What You See - B Is Higher And Faster**
Both start near 0 $\mu mol \, dm^{-3}$. Population B is always above A and its curve is steeper, meaning a higher rate of ATP production. The gap widens sharply after 5 min. Always separate description from explanation and give numbers.

Quote Paired Data With Units**
Pick like with like at the same time. For example at 4 min: B is about 40 and A is about 10 $\mu mol \, dm^{-3}$. At 6 min: B is about 100 and A is about 22 $\mu mol \, dm^{-3}$. At 7 min: B reaches about 120 while A stays at about 22 $\mu mol \, dm^{-3}$. That evidence earns credit for comparison.

Explain With Mitochondria**
Population B has mitochondria so it can complete aerobic respiration including the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Population A has no mitochondria so it cannot do oxidative phosphorylation. It is limited to glycolysis in the cytoplasm followed by ethanol fermentation in yeast, regenerating NAD to keep glycolysis going.

Link To ATP Yield**
Both make a small amount of ATP by substrate-linked phosphorylation in glycolysis, which is why A still rises a little then plateaus. B makes that plus a large extra yield from oxidative phosphorylation via chemiosmosis, so total ATP concentration and rate of increase are much greater.

Final answer: Population B produces more ATP and at a higher rate than A, e.g. at 6 min B approx 100 and A approx 22 $\mu mol \, dm^{-3}$ ATP; at 7 min B 120 and A 22 $\mu mol \, dm^{-3}$. B with mitochondria carries out glycolysis / substrate-linked phosphorylation plus oxidative phosphorylation (aerobic respiration). A without mitochondria carries out only glycolysis / anaerobic respiration / ethanol fermentation by substrate-linked phosphorylation, so cannot carry out oxidative phosphorylation.
